title: Lucido Spettoro
dek: An explorer and chronicler who asks what adventuring changes for a community, then carries the memory of earlier journeys into later choices.
sources: Deep character dossier · supplied 14 October 2026; quest evidence takes precedence
Selected primary scenes and established public histories; anchors below
body:
Lucido participates in events and records how he understands them. His journals preserve a person thinking about travel, institutions and ordinary lives, rather than an omniscient history of everything he witnesses.

August 2024 · money and local livelihoods

At a meeting with Pristinians he worries about the economic position adventurers have helped create. He encourages the party to patronize local businesses and asks whether local makers could compete with Zakar’s goods so that spending stays in town.

This is a proposal for capability and participation, not a confirmed new policy or completed manufacturing program. His concern places adventuring wealth inside the life of the settlement rather than treating purchases as an isolated personal decision.

The Rahu through a changing interpretation

His journal records gift exchange, hierarchy, Dasa and practices that initially trouble him. Those observations retain his perspective and do not settle every question about autonomy within the Rahu. His later declaration that he is Lucido of the Rahu is a consequential change in self-identification, not proof that every earlier objection was false.

A changing judgment belongs in the history. Neither the first moral reaction nor the later loyalty needs to become the Codex’s final verdict on a people.

2026 · the previous journey still matters

In later exploration he asks about a river’s role and history, compares the explanation with how rivers behave where he comes from and tests what the place is showing him. On another visit he says he would prefer to avoid the river because the last trip was difficult. Memory changes his next decision.

His humor remains visible beside that caution. A brief acceptance that it is time to fight can coexist with detailed questions about a route. The reflective chronicler is still an active companion.

The open record

His complete personal biography, the chronology of every journal entry and his full later Gael career remain only partly reconstructed. Civic proposals are not reported as enacted reforms, and journals do not turn impressions into objective fact.

Personal testimony: Lucido’s Rahu self-identification.

Recorded scenes

Dates identify transcript postings.

  • 8 August 2024 · local business proposal
  • 2 April 2026 · learning the river’s history
  • Testing the river account against experience
  • 9 April · remembering the earlier journey
  • 29 June · deciding to fight

Rehevä · a port home and a first voyage

At Eovar’s docks, Lucido is reminded of the port he calls home, Derlusk. He asks about landing places, fees, shallows and eddies, and recognizes why oars may be more useful than sails in narrow channels. He sounds informed enough that Dale asks about his experience.

Lucido admits that most of what he knows comes from sailors complaining in bars and restaurants: he has never actually gone to sea. He proposes learning together, then jokes that people who have never opened a book seem to manage sailing. Once seated at the bow, he tries to look as though he knows what he is doing.

He still takes part in steering the rented keelboat through the approaches. The voyage brings difficult current, rapids and an attack before the company finds shelter. Questions, borrowed knowledge and bluster accompany his practical contribution; the expedition does not retrospectively make him an experienced sailor before it begins.

Pristinia · learning to build

Lucido’s concern for local livelihoods leads into a trade. He says Jon has taken him on as an apprentice builder, and that he can start making houses when someone brings the materials. He has also sworn off Zakar’s shop for the foreseeable future after learning what effect adventurers’ spending has had on Pristinia.

He proposes using quarry stone for homes to show that the newcomers mean to stay. Those statements establish his apprenticeship and intended work, without converting every proposed house into a completed building. His later refugee work in Gael draws on a skill he has already begun developing here.

Gael · homes before a market

Seeing work on a market outside the Tower, Lucido objects that people still sleeping outside need homes first. Farkur answers with plans for fishing, paid work and a cycle of trade that could support both refugees and adventurers. He offers materials for a first house and a commission. They disagree over the order of the work, rather than over whether refugees should have shelter.

Lucido wants the building money paid to the refugees themselves. Their work aboard a wooden ship may give them useful skills, he argues, and wages would let them buy from the market. He offers to pay for help on two houses while acknowledging that materials and the remaining money are still a problem. His frustration includes a refusal to accept that there is another reasonable order of priorities; the exchange leaves that disagreement visible.

Later he reports three completed refugee homes and immediately says it is nowhere near enough. That is a specific report of progress, not a finished settlement or proof that he alone supplied its labor and resources. The Tower’s history preserves the continuing housing need alongside this contribution.
